one_liner: Maintained fork of lbzip2, a parallel bzip2-compatible compressor; single-threaded it already beats bzip2 1.0.8 by about 1.3x to 1.8x.
what_it_does: A command-line replacement for bzip2/bunzip2/bzcat (lbzip2, lbunzip2, lbzcat via symlinks) that reads and writes the standard .bz2 format byte-for-byte compatible with bzip2, using multiple worker threads (-n). The fork, created 2026-08-17 from kjn/lbzip2 commit 724352c, restores an optimised default CMake build, adds macOS and MSYS2 Windows builds, a working make install and SIMD speedups. It is a program, not a library: there is no installed libbz2-style API; lzbench reaches the internal encoder/decoder functions (encode.h, decode.h) through its own wrapper in bwt/lbzip2.
how_it_is_fast: The BWT is computed with divbwt, an induced-sorting suffix-array construction from Yuta Mori's libdivsufsort lineage, instead of bzip2's comparison-based block sort, so compression speed barely changes from -1 to -9 (22.0 vs 22.4 MB/s in lzbench 2.4) where bzip2 slows down. Huffman tables are built with length-limited minimum-redundancy coding (Larmore-Hirschberg, Moffat-Katajainen) and decoded table-driven (Liddell-Moffat). The fork adds a vectorised forward MTF (SSE2/NEON), an inverse MTF done with one byte shuffle (pshufb with SSSE3, vqtbl1q_u8 on AArch64), slice-by-8 CRC32 and four rotating frequency counters. On top of that, input blocks are compressed and decompressed in parallel across worker threads.
when_to_use: You must produce or consume .bz2 files (archives, distro packages, legacy pipelines) and want them faster without changing the format.
Multicore machines: the fork's README reports 220 MB compressing in 0.32 s on 18 cores versus 4.68 s single-threaded (Apple M5 Max), about 14.6x (derived from page data).
Replacing bzip2 in shell pipelines or tar (tar -I lbzip2) on Linux, macOS or MSYS2.
High levels (-9, 900k blocks) where bzip2 is slowest: lbzip2 keeps about 22 MB/s single-threaded versus 12.7 MB/s for bzip2 -9 on Silesia.
when_not_to_use: If you are free to choose the format: zstd, bzip3 or libbsc give better ratio and speed than any bzip2 implementation (bzip3 -5 reaches 22.29% and bsc -m0 23.26% on Silesia versus 25.75% for lbzip2 -9).
In-process compression from C/C++: there is no supported library API; use libbz2 or an embeddable codec instead.
Projects that cannot accept GPL-3.0-or-later code in the build or distribution.
Native Win32 builds: only the MSYS2 POSIX runtime (needs msys-2.0.dll) is supported.
Where long-term maintenance matters: the fork is one person's work since August 2026 (1 star, 0 forks); upstream kjn/lbzip2 is unmaintained.

integration.form: command-line tool (built from source with CMake; Homebrew tap caius72/lbzip2)
integration.dependencies: POSIX threads and POSIX runtime (fork, sigaction, sysconf); no external libraries
integration.platforms: Linux (glibc, musl), macOS on Apple Silicon, Windows via MSYS2; SIMD paths for x86-64 (SSE2; SSSE3 only when enabled at compile time) and AArch64 NEON, scalar fallback elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (standalone multithreaded program; thread count set with -n, capped at 1024 or 4x online CPUs)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: drop-in for the bzip2 command line and .bz2 format, not for the libbz2 C API

gotchas: Like bzip2, it deletes the input file after compressing unless -k or -c is given.
The SSSE3 inverse-MTF path compiles in only when the build already targets SSSE3 (-march=native or x86-64-v2); a default x86-64 build uses the slower branchy path.
--small is accepted but ignored (main.c: 'For now --small is ignored'), so memory use is not reduced.

Open upstream issues not listed as fixed in the fork's CHANGES.md: #35 (changes file permissions on files the user does not own), #27 (-n not working with tar) and #29 (lbzcat slower when the output file already exists).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick lbzip2 over bzip3, libbsc or zstd only when the output must stay in bzip2 format; those siblings win on ratio and speed with their own formats. Compared with pigz or Rapidgzip it is the analogous parallel tool for the .bz2 rather than .gz ecosystem.
verified_claims_summary: lzbench 2.4 (gcc 15.2.0 release binary, single thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.2 GHz, turbo off, silesia.tar) measured lbzip2 2.6.5 -1 at 22.0 MB/s compress and 62.7 MB/s decompress versus bzip2 1.0.8 -1 at 13.5 and 41.1 MB/s, and -9 at 22.4 and 47.0 versus 12.7 and 35.5 MB/s at the same 25.75% ratio (1.6-1.8x compress, 1.3-1.5x decompress, derived from page data). The fork's own README adds about 8% faster compression and 9% faster decompression over lbzip2 2.5 on an Apple M5 Max (first-party); most of the gain over bzip2 comes from upstream lbzip2's design, and lzbench's multithreaded table does not include lbzip2.
status_note: Active since August 2026 (2.6.5, last commit 2026-08-19) as the de facto maintained lbzip2 after Homebrew dropped the unmaintained upstream; GPL-3.0-or-later, CI on four platforms with 1111 tests, but a single maintainer.
